Semiconductor stocks lost around $1 trillion in market value on Friday, with Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) shares plunging over 28% in a day.

Intel’s fourth-quarter outlook landed well short of expectations, triggering the decline. Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. (NYSE:TSM) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) also declined, pushing the Nasdaq down 2.86%.

Jim Cramer’s Warning Amid Midterms, Earnings

"Mad Money" host Jim Cramer said Friday that Wall Street’s next stretch could stay jumpy, arguing investors are still wrestling with whether massive artificial intelligence outlays are paying off fast enough to support technology valuations.

Cramer on CNBC said that the coming week stacks several potential catalysts on top of an already shaky backdrop, including major earnings, the monthly jobs report and the midterm elections.

He urged investors not to get cute trying to time a tech bottom and instead focus on higher-quality names that may be getting sold indiscriminately.

"After a brutal week for tech, don’t assume the worst is behind us," Cramer said.

"Don’t try to call the bottom in the Nasdaq just yet. Pick up some high-quality companies that are being thrown away," he added.

Intel’s Pressure Point

One pressure point highlighted by Intel’s update is that booming data center demand does not automatically translate into smooth shipments when components are tight.

Intel’s Data Center and AI unit posted 78% revenue growth to $7.3 billion in the third quarter, but the company also pointed to wafer and substrate shortages that could limit server deliveries until the second half of 2027.

Analysts also tied Intel’s weakness to the PC market, where the company said high memory prices are making machines harder to sell at scale. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the roughly $17.1 billion consensus, and warned the slowdown could extend through the first half of 2027.

Can Upcoming Earnings Calm Market Anxiety?

Cramer’s calendar for the week ahead leans heavily on results from bellwether tech names, starting with Apple Inc.’s (NASDAQ: AAPL report Monday after the close. He said he still wants to own Apple, but also flagged that a valuation near 40 times earnings leaves little cushion if expectations are missed, according to the report.

Tuesday brings AMD’s earnings, which Cramer framed as another checkpoint for semiconductors after Intel’s stumble. In the same chip shockwave, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) sank 8% and the PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 7.1%, marking its second decline of more than 6% in a little over a week.

How Election Outcomes Could Impact Tech Investments

Cramer also put Tuesday’s midterm elections on his list of reasons volatility could linger, watching for any shift in Washington that might complicate data center development. He said political pushback against facilities could slow construction and hit businesses counting on AI infrastructure spending, while noting some states remain receptive.

Macro data could add another layer on Friday when the monthly jobs report arrives, which Cramer expects to show solid hiring but restrained wage growth.

news.content:
The AI skills gap in American workplaces may soon have less to do with who can write the smartest chatbot prompt and more to do with who can safely delegate work to software that can research, make critical decisions, and act.

That is the distinction Nate Herk, a 24-year-old Chicago-based AI automation creator and educator, sees emerging as businesses move from generative AI assistants toward autonomous agents.

"Someone who’s only learned to prompt a chatbot takes what the model gives them and passes it along," Herk said in an interview with Benzinga. An AI-ready worker, by contrast, can break a job into tasks, decide which should go to AI and "use their own expertise to check what comes back."

The gap matters as employers raise their expectations. A 2026 Harris Poll survey for Express Employment Professionals, a staffing and workforce-solutions company, found 93% of U.S. job seekers believe they possess the AI skills employers want. Still, only 35% think companies expect advanced or expert proficiency. Among hiring managers, 41% say candidates need skills at that level, while 90% look for at least basic AI proficiency.

AI Literacy Moves Beyond The Prompt

According to data from LinkedIn, the world’s largest online professional networking platform, demand is already headed in that direction. U.S. jobs requiring AI-literacy skills grew 70% year over year, LinkedIn said, while Gallup, an analytics and advisory company known for its workplace and public-opinion research, found in July that 52% of American employees used AI at work by mid-2026. Only 30%, however, used it a few times a week or more and 15% used it daily.

For Herk, a former Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.‘s (NYSE:GS) business-intelligence analyst, fluency means more than frequency.

"You should be able to explain why you used AI for a task and how you know the result is good," he said. "You can outsource the thinking, but you can’t outsource the understanding."

Research from Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), the technology giant behind the Copilot AI platform, points in much the same direction. Its 2026 Work Trend Index found 50% of surveyed AI users said quality control of AI output had become more important and 46% pointed to critical thinking. Some 86% said they treated AI output as a starting point rather than a final answer. Microsoft said workers are increasingly shifting from generating answers themselves toward "evaluating, refining, and owning" AI-generated work.

Read Also: AI Agent Testing Is Becoming A Major Bottleneck, Says Box CEO Aaron Levie, Calling Enterprise Deployment ‘Slow And Tedious’

The emphasis on judgment has also surfaced in warnings from former Microsoft Business Division President Jeff Raikes, who has argued that AI literacy without critical thinking could leave companies with a workplace skills problem if automation removes the entry-level experiences through which employees learn judgment.

That reinforces Herk’s argument that traditional workplace skills are changing rather than disappearing.

"If two people have those qualities and only one knows how to use AI well, I’m taking that person ten times out of ten," he said.

Agents Raise Stakes When They Act

The bigger shift comes when AI stops drafting and starts doing.

"The risk goes up exponentially," Herk said of agents that can send emails, update databases or make purchases. He recommends narrowly scoped permissions and human approval before actions that are difficult to reverse. "If you don’t want it sending emails, don’t give it permission to send emails."

That closely matches guidance from the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Foundation, a global nonprofit that develops open-source guidance to improve software security. OWASP warns against giving AI agents excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy and recommends human approval before high-impact actions.

But Yoshua Bengio, a pioneering artificial intelligence researcher and founder of nonprofit AI-safety research organization LawZero, takes the concern further. Bengio said at the United Nations Security Council in September that increasingly capable agents had already displayed dangerous behavior against instructions, including attempts to evade controls. His research argues that unchecked AI agency could create risks ranging from malicious misuse to loss of human control.

Herk sees a more immediate workplace failure in which an agent can follow instructions correctly and still produce a bad result because its underlying information was stale, contradictory or wrong.

"If you use a hundred agents to build something and it does well, you deserve the credit," he said. "If it goes wrong, you don’t get to say, ‘Well, the AI did it.’"

Experts Split On How Far Automation Goes

Herk also pushes back on promises that one autonomous system can replace an entire department.

"The claim I think is overhyped is, ‘One agent runs my whole marketing team,’" he said. "I automate tasks, not jobs."

That view has powerful supporters and equally prominent skeptics.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude family of models, has offered a much more disruptive forecast. He warned in 2025 that AI could eliminate as many as half of entry-level white-collar jobs within several years, particularly across technology, finance, law and consulting. Amodei argued that AI use would increasingly shift from helping employees work toward actually automating jobs.

Jensen Huang has publicly challenged that outlook. Huang said technological advances tend to create new work as productivity expands and argued companies will need people to manage growing fleets of AI agents. "I don’t know why AI companies are trying to scare us," Huang said while offering what he called a counter-view to predictions of widespread job losses.

The evidence so far remains mixed. Anthropic’s Economic Index initially found AI usage leaned toward augmenting workers rather than fully automating their tasks, while its 2026 research emphasizes substantial uncertainty around how quickly AI will ultimately affect employment and wages.

Herk advises job seekers to prove they can navigate that uncertainty instead of simply advertising familiarity with the newest tool. "Learn to think like a consultant," he said. "Figure out what’s slowing [a business] down, and solve that problem with as little AI as you need."

Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) stock has diverged from its Magnificent 7 peers as investors view it as a safer bet while artificial intelligence (AI) concerns persist. It ended last week at $344, just below its all-time high of $350 and about 41% above its lowest level this year.

In contrast, the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (CBOE: MAGS) has dropped in the last three consecutive weeks. It has fallen by over 8.25% from its peak this year. Top companies like Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG), and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) have slipped. 

Apple to Publish Earnings on Monday

Apple has done well this year and has overtaken Nvidia to become the biggest company in the world with a market capitalization of over $5.02 trillion.

Apple has drawn attention because of its limited exposure to the AI industry. Unlike other hyperscalers, it is not spending billions of dollars on AI infrastructure. Instead, the company has focused on its core products while dedicating some resources to improving Apple Intelligence.

Apple’s capital expenditure has been relatively small this year. It spent just $2.0 billion in the first quarter and $2.5 billion in the second quarter. In contrast, top hyperscalers are spending over $700 billion this year and are making negative free cash flow. As a result, the company’s free cash flow in the first half of the year stood at over $57 billion. 

Read Also: Micron, SanDisk, and Western Digital Remain in Bear Territory, But Key Catalysts Remain Intact

Apple will publish its earnings report on Monday, and analysts expect that its business did well in the September quarter. Benzinga data shows that analysts see the revenue coming in at $113.27 billion, up by 10.5% from a year earlier.

Apple has made some major announcements ahead of its earnings. It launched its Apple Duo phone, which has already sold out. It also launched the iPhone 18, with early metrics by Counterpoint Research showing that sales were higher than the previous models.  

Apple also launched its new MacBooks, which feature a touchscreen, with sales expected to do well over time. 

These events explain why analysts are bullish on the company. JPMorgan’s Samik Chatterjee hiked his target from $340 to $360, while Bernstein and Evercore maintained their outperform ratings. 

Options Market Points to an Apple Stock Jump

The options market suggests that Apple shares may jump after the earnings. The company has an implied volatility of 52.3%, much higher than its historical volatility of 16.1%.

It has a put/call ratio of less than 1, a sign that it has more calls than puts. Most of the calls are concentrated at $355, up modestly from the current $344. On the other hand, most of the puts are concentrated at $330, suggesting a 4% drop from the current level.

Technically, the stock has formed an ascending channel since July this year. It has also remained above the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA). Its lowest point in October coincided with the 50-day EMA. It has also remained above the Supertrend indicator.

The stock may resume the upward trend, potentially to the key resistance at $355. A drop below last Friday’s low of $334 will invalidate the bullish outlook.

A two-day tech rout erased more than $600 billion in market value from Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), as investors punished cash-draining AI spending.

Outside of Alphabet, that posted a second straight quarter of negative free cash flow (minus $9.1 billion, on $51.4 billion of capex), Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN) reported trailing 12-month free cash flow of negative $42.4 billion and still plans $220 billion of 2026 capex.

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), now cash flow negative, also joined Alphabet in a bear market.

“We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said according to CNN.

Margin Debt Rolls Over

In 2026, retail margin debt exploded to a record $1.502 trillion in June, then eased slightly to $1.48 trillion by September, FINRA data showed.

May’s record 53.7% annual growth rate was the fourth-highest since 1998, trailing only 2000, 2007 and 2021, and each of those peaks came before a market decline.

Falling collateral values can snowball into forced selling. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank 7.2% Friday, taking its October loss past 15%, as Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) fell 10.9%, Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) 11.1%, SanDisk 13.5% and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) 4.2%.

ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) lost about 30% over just two days, and Reddit (NYSE:RDDT) tumbled 29.2% as Google’s AI search ate into its traffic. A reported $6.3 billion Binance hack sent Coinbase Global (NASDAQ:COIN), Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) and Robinhood (NASDAQ:HOOD) down 7.2% to 10.6%.

CNBC reported BofA flagged widening high-yield spreads and a rotation into defensive stocks. Its derivatives strategists said that shift has pushed consumer staples and health care to “bubble-risk levels.” Exxon Mobil NYSE: XOM) rose 2.2% and Chevron (NYSE:CVX) 1.8%.

Hedging the Buildout

According to Bloomberg’s Matt Levine, someone has to own "a kajillion dollars of systematic data-center credit risk."

He argues these loans depend on AI tenants paying before the chips become obsolete. The market knows this, and its jitters pushed weekly credit-default swap trading tied to Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Nvidia over $9 billion in September, up from under $2 billion in July.

Five-year Oracle protection costs 3.3% a year, up tenfold in five years. Spreads widened even for Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), despite Microsoft’s $18.6 billion of free cash flow last quarter.

The S&P 493 Problem

Per Apollo’s Chief Economist Torsten Sløk, AI has delivered “zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech.” Revenue per worker and margins are rising for the Magnificent Seven but flat for the S&P 493.

His data showed the top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of model-serving spend and 95.6% of OpenAI and Anthropic spend, with VC-backed startups making up 80.4% of the top 1%. Non-VC firms are 86.9% of median spenders.

Sløk said mainstream companies increasingly view tokens “not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.”

The S&P 500, Dow Jones, and Nasdaq 100 have pulled back over the past few weeks as investors rotate out of their artificial intelligence (AI) bets. The Dow has dropped 5.35% from its year-to-date high, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have fallen 3.27% and 9.57%, respectively. This article looks at the top catalysts to watch this week.

US Stocks to React to Top Tech Earnings

The main theme in the market in the past three weeks has been corporate earnings from some of the biggest companies in the US. FactSet (NYSE:FDS) data shows that 60% of all companies in the S&P 500 Index have published their earnings, with the blended growth rate being 30%.

Earnings season picked up pace last week as Magnificent 7 members Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG), and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) released their results. Other major companies that reported included Intel, Eli Lilly, Chevron, ExxonMobil, and Mastercard.

The earnings season will continue this week, with some notable tech names publishing their numbers. Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) will release on Monday, while AMD and Arm Holdings will follow on Tuesday and Wednesday. These earnings will provide more details about the state of American companies. 

Read Also: NIO Stock Under Fire: Slowing October Deliveries Pile On the Pressure

US Nonfarm Payrolls Data

The three indices pulled back last week after the Federal Reserve delivered its interest rate decision on Thursday. As was widely expected, the bank left interest rates unchanged between 3.75% and 4%. Officials signaled that they will support hiking rates in the final meeting of the year. 

The most important macro data from the US will be the October jobs numbers. A report coming out on Friday is expected to show that the economy added 63k jobs last month after adding 29k in September. A stronger-than-expected report will raise the possibility of the Fed hiking rates.

These numbers come at a time when US bond yields have pulled back. The ten-year yield dropped to 4.929%, while the five-year dropped to 4.722%.

US Midterm Elections

The Dow Jones, Nasdaq 100, and S&P 500 indices will also react to this week’s midterm elections. Most polls show that Democrats will likely win the Senate and the House of Representatives. The same is true with traders on Polymarket and Kalshi. 

The outcome of this election will have some impact on the stock market. A Democratic sweep will likely lead to prolonged government shutdowns, gridlock in debt ceiling negotiations, and risks to the AI industry. 

US-Iran War and Impact on the Energy Market

US stocks will also react to the potential restart of the US-Iran war. The Trump administration has already told its Gulf allies to prepare for a short and intense war against Iran. Iran, on the other hand, has warned that it will respond harshly to any US attacks. 

Trump may decide to launch these strikes to distract from a Republican loss in the midterm elections. If the war starts, it will likely lead to more volatility in the stock market as oil prices rise.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) stock is stuck in a bear market as investors dump companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. It fell to $504 on Friday, 23.58% below its all-time high, with its market cap dropping to $824 billion from over $1.06 trillion in October. Will its upcoming earnings help turn the tide?

Advanced Micro Devices to Publish Earnings Amid Circular Investing Concerns

AMD will publish its financial results as investors remain concerned about several factors. One of these challenges is the circular nature of its investments. While Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is the best-known name in circular investments, AMD has done the same. 

The most recent one was its participation in Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) financing. It is investing $1 billion in the company, with Meta expected to use some of the proceeds to buy AMD’s CPUs, GPUs, and networking systems. Meta is already one of the biggest buyers of AMD’s products. 

AMD has also invested in Anthropic, the biggest AI lab in the world. It committed to investing $5 billion in Anthropic. Anthropic already uses AMD’s solutions to train its AI models. 

Read Also: NIO Stock Under Fire: Slowing October Deliveries Pile On the Pressure

AMD stock has also slumped as investors have dumped companies in the GPU industry. Last week, Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) had its worst daily performance ever after its earnings report disappointed. Nvidia has also dropped by double digits from its all-time high. 

It is against this backdrop that AMD will publish its quarterly earnings report. Based on the recent earnings reports by top companies in the AI industry like Micron, SanDisk, Samsung Electronics, and Samsung, chances are that AMD will publish strong earnings. 

Benzinga data shows that analysts expect AMD’s September quarter revenue to jump 41% to $13 billion. Earnings per share are expected to rise to $1.94 from $1.20 in the same quarter last year. Most of this growth will be driven by its AI business, including GPUs and CPUs.

AMD Stock is at Risk of Falling After Earnings

Recent history shows that most AI companies have fallen after releasing their earnings, including Intel, Micron, and SanDisk. This suggests investors have set a high bar for results and are still concerned about the AI bubble. 

The options market points to an AMD stock retreat after its earnings. It has a put/call open interest ratio of 1.03, a sign that it has more puts than calls. Most of the puts are at $490, about 3% below the current level.

On the charts, AMD has been in a slow downward trend in the past few weeks, moving from a high of $660 in October to the current $504. It made a brief pullback, reaching a high of $577 last week, and then it dropped. 

The stock has dropped below the 23.6% Fibonacci Retracement level. It has slumped below the 50-day moving average, while the Supertrend indicator has turned red. Therefore, the stock will likely drop further, potentially to the 50% retracement level of $421, down by 16.25% from the current level.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) has slumped into a bear market, falling from a record high of $656 in June to $471, its lowest level since July. This retreat has coincided with the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) bubble fears that have affected most semiconductor companies. 

SOXX, which tracks the biggest semiconductor companies, has dropped as most of its constituent firms tumble. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD), its biggest constituent, has dropped by 23.20% from its peak this year. 

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has fallen by 16% from its peak, while Micron (NASDAQ:MU), Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO), and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) have all fallen into a technical bear market.

These stocks have dropped as investors remain concerned about the AI industry continuing to rise. Investors are concerned that this could be one of the biggest bubbles in history. Ray Dalio, Michael Burry, and Ken Griffin have all warned that the bubble may burst as interest rates and bond yields rise. 

These concerns have risen in the past few weeks. OpenAI, the AI pioneer, is said to have raised just $11 billion, much lower than the $30 billion it was targeting. It also reduced its targeted valuation from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion.

Other AI companies are also struggling. For example, top neocloud companies like CoreWeave, Nebius, Riot Platforms, and IREN have all plunged, with Elon Musk warning that over 200 neocloud companies will go under as funding dries. All these events will have an impact on semiconductor companies in the SOXX ETF. 

These fears explain why investors have started selling their SOXX shares. The fund experienced a $1.54 billion in outflows on Friday, bringing its assets under management to $48 billion.

President Donald Trump defended Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang after a report that a suspected Chinese spy targeted the executive, though he said the administration will take a closer look at the allegations.

Administration Reviewing the Report

The New York Times reported on Thursday that U.S. officials determined a Singapore-based executive with close ties to Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Asked about it on Saturday at a Halloween event at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida, Trump said he has “a lot of respect for Jensen” but “didn’t know about the specific thing.”

“He’s a great, brilliant person, and we want to protect our brilliant people,” Trump added.

He said that his administration would look at the allegations “very closely.”

Read Also: Trump Reveals US Probing $6.3 Billion Binance Crypto Hack As North Korea-Linked Hackers Come Under Suspicion, Says Exchange Told Officials Situation Is ‘Pretty Much Under Control’

Report Says Trump Was Briefed Last Year

Surveillance reportedly documented a close relationship between her and the Nvidia CEO and Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago but decided against acting, according to the report.

An Nvidia spokesperson told Benzinga that Megaspeed is “no different than many other regional cloud customers” and that the diversion allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”

Huang’s Advisory Role

Huang sits on the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

Asked whether he would stay on, Trump said he would “like to say yes” unless “we find out something to the contrary.”

“I’ve always found Jensen Huang to be very aboveboard. But, you know, you’re dealing in a very complex issue,” he added.

Last week, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called on Huang and Nvidia’s board to answer to Congress, months after inviting him to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Nvidia’s China sales.

“We have been losing money for many years with Canada,” Trump said.

He added that “we are now very close to having a deal” after two conversations with his Canadian counterpart last week.

In a post on X, Carney described a “good conversation” with Trump on the future of trade, adding that their teams will now work “in the coming weeks” toward a deal that creates jobs, boosts affordability and respects Canada’s culture and sovereignty.

Pfizer Inc (NYSE:PFE) investors may be eyeing potential gains from the company’s dividends ahead of its third-quarter report on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Currently, Pfizer has an annual dividend yield of 5.64%, with a quarterly dividend of 43 cents per share ($1.72 a year). So, how can investors exploit its dividend yield to pocket a regular $500 monthly?

To earn $500 per month or $6,000 annually from dividends alone, you would need an investment of about $106,454 or around 3,488 shares. For a more modest $100 per month or $1,200 per year, you would need $21,303 or around 698 shares.

To Calculate

Divide the desired annual income ($6,000 or $1,200) by the dividend ($1.72 in this case). So, $6,000 / $1.72 = 3,488 shares ($500 per month), and $1,200 / $1.72 = 698 shares ($100 per month).

Note that dividend yield can change on a rolling basis, as dividend payments and stock prices both fluctuate over time.

How It Works

The dividend yield is computed by dividing the annual dividend payment by the stock’s current price.

For example, if a stock pays an annual dividend of $2 and trades at $50, the dividend yield is 4% ($2/$50). However, if the stock price increases to $60, the dividend yield drops to 3.33% ($2/$60). Conversely, if the stock price falls to $40, the dividend yield rises to 5% ($2/$40).

Similarly, changes in dividend payments can affect yield. If a company increases its dividend, the yield will also increase, provided the stock price stays the same. Conversely, if the dividend payment decreases, the yield will too.

Analysts expect earnings of 41 cents per share on $2.18 billion in revenue, up 84% year over year. Earnings Whispers puts the unofficial hurdle at 49 cents.

On Kalshi, traders are betting on which words CEO Alex Karp and his team will say during the 5 p.m. ET call.

What Kalshi Predicts Palantir Will Say

“International” and “Maven” lead at 98% each.

CFO David Glazer routinely breaks out overseas commercial and government revenue. International business supplied about 19% of sales last quarter, while international commercial revenue grew 26%, versus 149% for U.S. commercial.

The Pentagon is making Maven a core military intelligence program. “TITAN” sits at 58% after the Army awarded Palantir $127 million for battlefield targeting systems.

“Revenue Guidance” trades at 87%. Palantir raised its 2026 sales forecast by $500 million to $8.15 billion in August, implying 82% annual growth. Investors are looking for another increase.

“Sovereign AI” stands at 86%. After going unmentioned on seven consecutive calls, the phrase appeared eight times in August as Palantir pushed customers to control their AI models and data.

“Nvidia” trades at 61%. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) supplies AI chips and models used with Palantir’s software, while also deploying that software to manage its own supply chain. The companies are jointly marketing the technology to other businesses.

What Kalshi Predicts Palantir Will Skip

“Nebius” is nearly a coin flip at 49%, despite Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS) becoming Palantir’s preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner.

“Slop” trades at 42%. Executives used the term 17 times in May to attack AI output with little business value, but only once in August.

“Warp Speed” sits at 37%. The manufacturing software was mentioned on seven consecutive earnings calls before disappearing in August.

“Commercial Growth” trades at 31%. Executives discussed U.S. commercial revenue growth in August without saying those exact words.

“Anthropic / Claude” stands at 11%. Asked in August about AI models being pulled, after the Pentagon ordered Claude’s removal from Maven, Karp answered without naming Anthropic.

The Valuation Debate

JPMorgan analyst Brian Essex sees a business already delivering returns on AI investment, setting a $262 price target. RBC analyst Rishi Jaluria is far less optimistic, maintaining a $90 target on valuation concerns.

Against Friday’s closing price of $184.11, those targets imply roughly 42% upside or 51% downside.

Unlike AI data-center builders facing mounting financing problems, Palantir is already generating substantial cash. It produced $1.22 billion in adjusted free cash flow last quarter.

At Friday’s close, investors valued Palantir at roughly 53 times its expected 2026 revenue, leaving little room for disappointment.

‘Big Short’ investor Steve Eisman warned that falling AI prices, moderating usage and data-center obstacles could expose weaknesses across the stock market, where AI has become a dominant investment theme.

Eisman discussed the risks during a podcast, Behind the Business with Michelle Toh, last week. Eisman said OpenAI recently lowered the price of its latest model after computing capacity increased substantially. That move could put pressure on Anthropic to reduce prices as well, intensifying competition among leading AI developers.

He also pointed to the retreat from "token maxing," a practice in the recent past wherein companies encouraged employees to use AI extensively regardless of expense. Eisman said businesses are increasingly focused on controlling costs and evaluating whether usage produces measurable value.

Eisman said financial disclosures from OpenAI and Anthropic could become more transparent if either company goes public. He suggested Anthropic might pursue a listing before weaker growth figures potentially affect investor interest.

The investor said AI influences more than half the stock market when technology companies outside the information technology sector are included. Consumer staples, health care and real estate are the least connected sectors, while utilities, banks and industrial companies remain linked through power, financing and construction.

Eisman warned that an AI downturn could extend beyond a recession and trigger a "massive correction" in stocks. He cited pricing pressure, slower token usage and permitting challenges affecting data-center construction.

Read Also: Midterms Could Set Up Another S&P 500 Rally, but Investors May Be Missing the Bigger Opportunity — Strategist Sees Stock Market Correction Nearing Its End as Breadth Improves

AI Spending Risks Could Trigger Recession

Speaking about the economy, Eisman argued that the AI boom is built on a highly concentrated chain of spending, making it vulnerable to financial trouble at OpenAI or Anthropic.

Citing Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) as an example, the company stated that its revenue growth of more than 100% masks customer concentration, with 70% of its accounts receivable coming from just five customers, according to its 10-Q filing. Meanwhile, OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly account for a significant share of hyperscalers’ AI revenue, driving their massive chip purchases.

He warned that financial trouble at either AI startup could disrupt the entire chain, hurting hyperscalers, Nvidia and companies such as Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL), which reportedly has roughly half of its $600 billion backlog tied to OpenAI, thus cautioning that a reversal in AI spending could have broader economic consequences, potentially pushing the U.S. into a “recession immediately.”

AI CapEx Faces a Reality Check

Last week, Apollo Global Management Chief Economist Torsten Slok said that AI’s financial benefits remain concentrated among large technology companies, with little evidence of broader productivity gains across corporate America. Slok found that technology companies’ revenue per employee rose from roughly $550,000 in 2022 to nearly $800,000, while the figure remained largely unchanged for the rest of the S&P 500. Tech profit margins also expanded, but margins across other sectors stayed near 10%.

Meanwhile, Yorkville America CEO Steve Neamtz told Benzinga that investors are increasingly scrutinizing whether surging AI capital expenditures are translating into measurable revenue growth and returns. He said demand, financing, power availability, customer commitments and capacity utilization will determine the sustainability of infrastructure spending.

On Polymarket, traders still give Nvidia a 56% chance of finishing 2026 as the world’s most valuable company, against Apple’s 44%.

Tastytrade founder Tom Sosnoff expects the pullback in the market’s most crowded chip stocks to continue, telling CNBC Monday morning that the rally’s biggest winners have yet to fall anywhere close to oversold levels. 

The big names at "the top of the funnel"—pointing to Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) and Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU)—are carrying the broader market, he said.

The problem? When leadership is this narrow, and such a small group of tech stocks powers a large share of the market’s gains, as has been the case in recent years, weakness in a few names can drag on major indexes more than usual.

  • NVDA stock is moving Monday. See the chart and price action here.

Read Also: Bears Load Up on Ondas, Dutch Bros and 8 More Stocks — Is a Squeeze Brewing?

Intel Stands Apart

Sosnoff argues that the recent declines in Nvidia, AMD and Micron have been sharp but not deep enough to wash out the excess. Before he calls any of them oversold, he wants to see a 25% to 35% drop. Anything less, in his framework, still looks like an ordinary pullback for stocks with such large runs behind them.

Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) is the exception in Sosnoff’s view. The tech company’s shares, trading around $65 after its own selloff, are arguably already oversold.

Intel shares plunged 28.58% on Friday, one of the steepest single-day drops in the company’s history, and were trading near $65 on Monday, per Benzinga Pro data. The collapse helps explain why Sosnoff views Intel as arguably oversold while still expecting more downside in Nvidia, AMD and Micron. 

A Choppy Week Ahead

Sosnoff expects trading this week to be "choppy" and cautioned against chasing Monday morning’s rebound, saying the bounce was a hard spot to buy.

Better opportunities, he suggested, are more likely to appear around midweek, when oversold conditions in individual names could set up cleaner entry points. 

Timing matters in his playbook. Waiting a day or two for sellers to exhaust themselves can produce a far better price than jumping in on the first green candle.

His outlook reflects his background. Sosnoff co-founded the thinkorswim trading platform before launching tastytrade, and both businesses center on options trading, volatility and active risk management. His calls tend to focus on price levels and probabilities rather than long-term conviction on a single company.

What Traders Are Watching

The key question is whether chip leaders can find support or whether Sosnoff’s 25% to 35% threshold comes into play. A decline of that size in Nvidia, AMD and Micron would mark a significant reset for the stocks most responsible for the market’s gains.

Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) headline a crowded week of earnings, with both on Monday’s calendar and AMD scheduled to follow after Tuesday’s close, giving traders a fresh read on tech demand after disappointing reports from Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) rattled the sector last week.

Traders will be watching Monday’s and midweek price action closely for signs of capitulation, including heavy volume and sharp intraday reversals. Sosnoff’s read suggests any real bottom in the group is still some distance away.

Semiconductor stocks are experiencing a dramatic valuation reset, potentially creating an opportunity for investors seeking exposure to the AI trade through ETFs.

The S&P 500 Semiconductors Index’s forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio fell to 14.7x on October 30, down from approximately 33x a year earlier, according to LSEG data. The multiple is now below the S&P 500’s forward P/E of 18.9x, reversing the premium semiconductor stocks commanded during much of the AI rally.

The correction has hit semiconductor ETFs particularly hard. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) plunged 8.24% on Friday, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) fell 6.98%. The SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (NYSE:XSD) declined 6.30%. SOXX, SMH and XSD lost 17.1%,14.2%, 14.6%, respectively, during October.

Read Also: Black Friday Came Early for Chipmakers: Intel and 10 Other Stocks Are More Than 20% Off This Month

SOXX Vs. SMH: Portfolio Concentration Matters

The selloff also highlights differences in how semiconductor ETFs distribute their exposure.

SOXX has 34 holdings, with Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) accounting for 9.24% of its portfolio, Intel Corp (NASDAQ:INTC), 6.33%, Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) 7.98%, Micron Technology, Inc (NASDAQ:MU) 7.95% and Broadcom, Inc (NASDAQ:AVGO) 7.58%. Its exposure to Nvidia and AMD makes it particularly sensitive to weakness among these chipmakers. In October, Nvidia retreated more than 10% and AMD, 17.5%.

SMH, with 26 holdings, is considerably more concentrated in leading semiconductor companies. Nvidia represents approximately 20.19% of its portfolio, followed by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) (9.58%), Texas Instruments Inc (NASDAQ:TXN) (5.70%), Broadcom (5.61%) and AMD (5.34%).

This concentration helped SMH outperform SOXX during the October 30 selloff, partly because Intel accounted for just 3.07% of SMH’s portfolio.

XSD offers a different approach through a more evenly distributed portfolio. However, its 6.30% single-day decline on Friday demonstrates that diversification within the semiconductor industry cannot eliminate sector-wide risks.

Is the Valuation Reset a Buying Opportunity?

The latest correction followed disappointing guidance from Intel, alongside growing concerns about the sustainability of massive AI infrastructure investments. Intel shares plunged 28.6% on October 30, while AMD dropped 10.9% and Nvidia declined 4.2%.

For SOXX, resistance levels appear to be forming near the $530 mark, according to Benzinga Pro, where the stock has previously encountered selling pressure. If the price can break through this level, it may signal a shift in momentum, potentially attracting more buyers and leading to further gains.

For XSD, support levels appear to be forming around the recent closing price of $452.10, which may serve as a critical point for buyers looking to enter the market. Should the price dip below this level, it could trigger further selling pressure, pushing the ETF closer to the lower end of its 52-week range. Resistance is likely near $471.49, where the ETF has struggled to maintain upward momentum. A sustained break above this threshold could signal a shift in market sentiment and potentially attract more bullish investors.

However, technical indicators analyzed by Benzinga suggest that SMH is in a cautious position. While it has shown resilience above the recent support level, the distance to resistance suggests further bullish momentum will require stronger catalysts.

Bottom Line

For semiconductor ETF investors, the decline in forward valuations could present an opportunity if earnings growth remains resilient. However, a lower P/E does not automatically mean stocks are undervalued. Downward revisions to earnings estimates could undermine the apparent valuation discount.

The next catalysts will be hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, semiconductor earnings revisions and demand trends across AI chips, memory and data-center infrastructure.

For SOXX, SMH and XSD investors, the key question is no longer whether semiconductor valuations have corrected, but whether earnings can justify buying the sector at these lower multiples.

Melius Research reiterated its Buy rating on Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) while lowering its price target to $315 per share from $420, CNBC reported Monday. The new target sits 25% below the old one.

Nvidia had company. Melius also reduced targets on Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD), Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO), Marvell Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MRVL), Dell Technologies Inc. (NYSE:DELL), Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) and CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV).

  • NVDA stock is climbing Monday. Get all the details here.

A Flood of Paper

The primary warning in the note concerned the sheer volume of securities headed to market.

According to the firm, "at least 5 trillion-dollar plus companies … have to issue hundreds of billions in securities." Melius added, "The amount of paper is so large it has become the primary risk."

Heavy issuance creates a supply problem for markets. Every new bond or share sale competes for the same pool of investor capital, which can weigh on prices across a sector. Chip suppliers would feel the effect secondhand, since their largest customers would be paying for orders with borrowed or newly raised money.

Few analysts have framed the AI trade around financing quite so bluntly. Most of the debate over the past year has focused on demand, supply constraints and whether spending would translate into profits. 

Melius moved the spotlight to the balance sheet side of the equation.

Read Also: AMD, Micron Selloff Is 'Just the Beginning,' Tom Sosnoff Says

Pressure on Multiples

Valuation drove the price target cuts. In its note, the firm said it was lowering targets "as multiples may remain under pressure as the buildout will feature more backstops throughout 2028."

In financing terms, a backstop is a commitment from one party to cover funding or absorb losses if other sources fall short. Melius appears to expect more of the AI infrastructure buildout to lean on such arrangements over the next two years. 

Structures of that kind can make investors more cautious about paying premium multiples, even with revenue still rising.

See More: Top Growth Stocks

Three of the seven companies face an added hit. Melius trimmed PC- and smartphone-related estimates at AMD, Dell and Qualcomm, according to CNBC. Weaker consumer device demand would land on top of the valuation pressure facing the broader data center trade.

The Buy rating on Nvidia stands. The lower target reflects a reset in what Melius believes investors will pay for chip earnings across the group, with the 2028 time frame suggesting the firm expects the pressure to linger.

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) is facing growing investor scrutiny over the cost of its AI buildout as rising capital commitments, equity issuance and weaker free cash flow raise questions about how quickly the company can convert heavy spending into returns.

S&P Flags Credit Risk As AI Spending Rises

S&P Global Ratings lowered the outlook on Meta’s AA- credit rating to negative, citing rising leverage and uncertainty over how long elevated capital spending and negative free operating cash flow could persist.

S&P said Meta has more limited visibility into AI monetization than some peers and questioned when new AI investments will begin producing revenue that materially exceeds their costs.

The rating firm expects Meta’s capital expenditures to reach about $140 billion in 2026 and rise above $225 billion in 2027. It also projects leverage could climb above 1.0 times next year from roughly 0.1 times last year.

Meta disagreed with S&P’s assessment. Company spokesperson Kamran Mumtaz told Bloomberg on Friday that Meta sees significant product and business opportunities ahead and believes its credit profile remains very strong.

Future Commitments And Equity Raise Add Pressure

Meta has disclosed more than $800 billion in future spending commitments, with nearly half tied to leases that have not yet started, largely for data centers and energy infrastructure.

CFO Susan Li said Meta expects to continue investing aggressively across its core business and emerging AI initiatives.

Meta also recently completed a $25 billion stock sale at $625 per share, while maintaining an at-the-market program that could sell up to another $60 billion of stock.

The stock fell below the offering price during Friday trading, adding to concerns around funding needs and shareholder dilution.

The stock has also reversed the gains that followed Meta’s September launch of Muse, its personal AI agent, Bloomberg reported on Friday. Meta continues exploring monetization opportunities around Muse and other AI products through subscriptions, transaction fees and potentially advertising.

The company is also developing a possible cloud business that could sell access to AI models or raw computing capacity.

Baruch Trims Meta On CapEx Headwinds

Blue Line Capital founder and president Bill Baruch said he reduced Meta to 1.5% of his portfolio from 2.5%.

Baruch told CNBC last Wednesday that the company’s capital-spending outlook has become a major headwind, pointing to expected 2026 capex of $135 billion to $145 billion and estimates approaching $200 billion for 2027.

He also highlighted negative free cash flow and said the stock failed to sustain momentum following the Muse launch and earnings.

Baruch said his firm is raising cash to maintain flexibility and chose Meta as one position to reduce.

Brown Keeps Meta Out Of His Portfolio List

Ritholtz Wealth Management CEO Josh Brown also turned more cautious on Meta for the intermediate term.

Brown removed Meta from his "Best Stocks in the Market" list after the stock weakened following its Muse-driven rally, equity issuance and renewed questions about AI funding.

He told CNBC on Tuesday that he would not re-enter the stock unless it reclaimed its 50-day moving average near $664.

Brown said Meta may still work as a long-term holding, but for now he sees too many stronger stocks elsewhere to focus on when Meta might rebound.

META Price Action: Meta Platforms shares were up 0.61% at $618.77 at the time of publication on Monday, according to Benzinga Pro data.

Hark is entering the consumer AI race with heavyweight backing: Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.’s (NASDAQ:AMD) AMD Ventures joined a $700 million round valuing it at $6 billion.

Now its founder, Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock, is pointing frustrated Grok Bot users toward Hark, turning complaints about Elon Musk‘s AI agent into an opening for a well-funded challenger.

Nvidia and AMD Back a Different AI Bet

Hark announced in May that it had raised more than $700 million in a Series A at a $6 billion post-money valuation. Led by Parkway Venture Capital, the round also included Intel Corp‘s (NASDAQ:INTC) Intel Capital, Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) Qualcomm Ventures, ARK Invest and Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) Salesforce Ventures.

Hark is not simply building another chatbot. It is developing its own foundation models, software and AI-native hardware, aiming to create a personal assistant that can act across the services people already use.

Its ambitions extend beyond answering questions. Hark wants its assistant to manage calendars, order groceries, book flights, summarize Slack conversations and operate a cloud computer to complete web-based tasks. The idea is to make AI less of a tool users consult and more of an assistant they delegate work to.

That broader vision helps explain why semiconductor investors are paying attention. Building and operating increasingly capable AI assistants requires computing infrastructure, while Hark’s ambitions around its own hardware could create another layer of opportunity.

Read Also: Elon Musk Has an AI Problem: People Are Using Grok Too Much

Grok’s Usage Problem Opens a Door

Hark’s competitive ambitions came into sharper focus on Nov. 2, when Adcock encouraged users frustrated by Grok Bot’s usage limits to try Hark, describing its subscription tiers as “incredibly generous.”

The endorsement is notable because Adcock is not just promoting a competing chatbot. He is positioning Hark as an alternative for users who want an AI assistant they can rely on for everyday tasks. It also puts the startup in the same consumer AI conversation as Musk’s Grok, which Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) said had reached 800,000 paid weekly users in its third quarter.

Hark’s funding gives it considerable financial backing to pursue that opportunity. Its investor roster also spans several major semiconductor companies, including Nvidia, AMD and Qualcomm, giving the startup connections across the infrastructure powering the AI industry.

A Bigger Bet on AI Assistants

For Nvidia and AMD, Hark represents more than a startup investment. The company is betting that consumers will increasingly delegate everyday digital work to AI agents, creating demand for models, infrastructure and eventually new hardware.

But a $6 billion valuation sets a high bar. Hark must turn its generous usage pitch into durable customer adoption while managing the same inference costs now confronting Grok. The opportunity is clear; whether its economics prove more sustainable remains the bigger test.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) faces its biggest test of the year as the U.S. midterms arrive Tuesday, with bulls arguing the bottom is already in while bears still eye $73,000 as a key downside target.

Why Bulls Say Bitcoin Won’t Fall Further

Widely-followed market commentator Our Crypto Talk posted on X that Bitcoin bottomed 71 days after the 2014 midterms, 39 days after 2018, and just 13 days after 2022, a shrinking window the account says points to Bitcoin already finding its low this cycle. 

"We don’t see it going below $58K at all, and we’d be very surprised if it did," the post read, citing Bitcoin’s resilience following this week’s Binance hack as further evidence.

Meanwhile, DWF Labs posted on X that Bitcoin gained in the 12 months following each of the last three midterm elections, rising 25%, 45% and 92% respectively, even though the path included drawdowns of 31% and 46% three months into the 2014 and 2018 cycles. 

The post also noted the third year of a presidential term has historically been the strongest for the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY), gaining in 17 of the last 19 cycles with an 18.9% median return, a pattern Bitcoin has mirrored with gains of 34% in 2015, 92% in 2019 and 155% in 2023.

Why Bears Still Point to $73,000

Widely-followed cryptocurency analyst Ali Martinez posted on X in late September that Bitcoin fell 72%, 65%, 52% and 27% following the 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022 midterms respectively, calling the pattern worth watching even though it doesn’t prove elections directly cause the declines. 

He flagged Bitcoin’s short-term holder cost basis near $73,000 as the key level to watch, since that zone has historically held through major corrections during confirmed bull markets.

Why $176 Million in Crypto Money Is Riding on Tuesday’s Races

Milk Road Crypto posted on X that crypto industry groups have poured roughly $176 million into the 2026 midterms across more than 100 races, with Fairshake and its affiliates accounting for $150.8 million of that total through October 20. 

Backers include Coinbase (NASDAQ:COIN), Ripple (CRYPTO: XRP) and a16z, following the same playbook that saw Fairshake spend $196 million in 2024. 

So far, 53 of the group’s 58 backed candidates have won their primaries or special elections.

The single biggest bet has landed in Ohio, where crypto groups have spent more than $68 million opposing Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown in his Senate race against Republican Jon Husted. 

With the Clarity Act stalled in Congress, JPMorgan analysts warned that a future administration could reverse federal agency rules, leaving the fight over who ultimately sets crypto policy unresolved heading into Election Day.
